question: Sampling
content: Sampling involves selecting a representative subset from a larger population to estimate characteristics of the whole. Reliability depends on sample size, random selection, and minimizing selection bias.
description: A political poll surveys 1,000 registered voters and predicts a candidate will win 52% to 48%. The actual election result is 51% to 49%. How did a sample of only 1,000 accurately predict millions of votes?
options: The pollsters were lucky to pick the right voters
A well-constructed random sample of sufficient size can reliably estimate population parameters
1,000 voters is a large enough sample to guarantee accuracy in any election
The poll surveyed an equal number of Democrats and Republicans
answer: A well-constructed random sample of sufficient size can reliably estimate population parameters
explanation: With random sampling and proper methodology, a relatively small sample can produce accurate estimates due to the law of large numbers and the Central Limit Theorem.

question: Selection Bias
content: Selection bias occurs when the sample is not representative of the population because of how participants are chosen, leading to systematically skewed results regardless of sample size.
description: In 1936, The Literary Digest polled over 2 million people and predicted Alf Landon would win the presidency. Franklin D. Roosevelt won in a landslide. What went wrong despite the massive sample?
options: 2 million is not a large enough sample for a national election
The sample drew from phone directories and car registrations, skewing toward the wealthy — massive selection bias
People lied to the pollsters about their voting intentions
The poll was conducted too far before the election
answer: The sample drew from phone directories and car registrations, skewing toward the wealthy — massive selection bias
explanation: No amount of sample size can fix a biased sampling method. The Literary Digest’s sample was unrepresentative because only wealthier citizens had phones and cars in 1936. Selection bias rendered the data worthless.

question: Central Limit Theorem
content: As sample size increases, the distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution regardless of the shape of the population distribution. This enables statistical inference from samples.
description: A population of website visit durations is highly skewed — most visits are under 2 minutes but a few last hours. Yet if you take many samples of 30+ visits and plot their averages, the averages form a bell curve. What theorem explains this?
options: The law of diminishing returns
The Central Limit Theorem — sample means approach normality regardless of population shape
Regression to the mean of visit durations
The law of large numbers only applies to large samples
answer: The Central Limit Theorem — sample means approach normality regardless of population shape
explanation: The Central Limit Theorem is what makes sampling work. Even from a skewed or bizarrely shaped population, the averages of sufficiently large samples will be approximately normally distributed.

question: Sample Size vs Accuracy
content: Beyond a certain point, increasing sample size yields diminishing returns in accuracy. The key factor is sample quality (randomness, representativeness), not absolute size.
description: A market research firm offers two options: survey 500 carefully selected random customers for $10,000, or survey 50,000 self-selected website visitors for $5,000. Which is likely more reliable?
options: The 50,000 survey — larger sample always means better accuracy
The 500 carefully selected random sample — representativeness matters more than raw size
Both are equally reliable since sample size is sufficient in both cases
Neither is reliable — you need at least 100,000 responses
answer: The 500 carefully selected random sample — representativeness matters more than raw size
explanation: A self-selected sample of 50,000 can have huge selection bias (only people with strong opinions respond). A well-constructed random sample of 500 is more representative and produces more accurate estimates.

question: Representation Rule
content: When collecting data for strategic decisions, prioritize the integrity and randomness of the sample over its sheer size. Ensure test cohorts accurately mirror the diverse profiles of the actual end-user base.
description: A company wants to launch a product globally but only surveys existing customers in San Francisco. According to the representation rule, what is the problem?
options: San Francisco customers differ from the global market — the sample is biased
San Francisco is too expensive for survey research
Existing customers cannot provide reliable feedback
The sample size from a single city is too small
answer: San Francisco customers differ from the global market — the sample is biased
explanation: If your target population is global buyers, sampling only from San Francisco introduces geographic, economic, and cultural selection bias. The conclusions cannot be generalized beyond that narrow segment.

question: A/B Testing Sampling
content: A/B testing is a controlled sampling experiment where users are randomly assigned to control and treatment groups to measure the causal effect of a change.
description: A website changes its checkout button color from blue to green. Week one uses green and conversions drop 10%. Week two reverts to blue and conversions return to normal. What is missing from this test?
options: The test ran for too short a duration
No simultaneous control group — day-of-week effects could explain the difference, not the color change
Green is an objectively worse color for buttons
The conversion metric was miscalculated
answer: No simultaneous control group — day-of-week effects could explain the difference, not the color change
explanation: True A/B testing requires random assignment of users to both versions simultaneously. Sequential testing confounds the change with time-based factors. Proper sampling requires concurrent control and treatment groups.

question: Destructive Sampling
content: In some contexts, sampling is destructive — testing destroys the item. Therefore, sample size must be carefully balanced to ensure confidence without excessive waste.
description: A bulletproof vest manufacturer must test that vests stop bullets. Each test destroys a vest. How should they determine the number of vests to test from each production batch?
options: Test every single vest to guarantee quality
Use statistical sampling — test a random sample to estimate the failure rate with acceptable confidence
Test only one vest per batch to minimize waste
Do not test any vests and rely on the manufacturing process
answer: Use statistical sampling — test a random sample to estimate the failure rate with acceptable confidence
explanation: When testing destroys the product, sampling is the only option. Statistical methods determine the minimum sample size needed to achieve a given confidence level in the quality estimate.

question: Sampling Error
content: Sampling error is the difference between the sample estimate and the true population value. It decreases as sample size increases but never reaches zero — there is always uncertainty.
description: A poll of 1,000 voters reports a 3% margin of error. What does the 3% represent?
options: The pollsters made a mistake in 3% of the calls
The true population value lies within 3% of the reported number 95% of the time
3% of voters are undecided and could change the outcome
The poll is 97% accurate and 3% inaccurate
answer: The true population value lies within 3% of the reported number 95% of the time
explanation: Margin of error quantifies sampling uncertainty. It means if the same poll were repeated 100 times, the result would fall within ±3% of the true population value 95 times. It is a measure of precision, not accuracy.
